title: Take and read
hookLine: in a Milan garden Augustine hears a child's voice say take and read, and his long restlessness ends (Confessions 8)

cards: Tomorrow is a very comfortable word. The habit you'll quit tomorrow. And then tomorrow.

Milan. Augustine is a successful teacher of speaking, career on the rise, and he is falling apart. He's become convinced the faith his mother prayed for is true, but he can't make himself step into it.
He writes that he was bound, not by iron chains, but by his own will. One day, with his friend Alypius, in the garden of the house where they're staying, it all comes to a head.
He goes off alone under a fig tree, throws himself down, and weeps. How long? Tomorrow, and tomorrow?

teach.b: Then, Augustine says, he heard a voice from a house next door, like a child's, chanting over and over: take up and read, take up and read. In Latin, tolle lege.
He stops crying and tries to think of any children's game that uses those words. He can't, so he takes it as a command.
He remembers Antony, the desert monk, who once walked into church, heard a Gospel line read aloud, and took it as spoken to him.

teach.h: THE FIRST THING HIS EYES FALL ON.
teach.b: So Augustine hurries back to where Alypius is sitting, where he'd left a book of Paul's letters, snatches it up, and reads the first thing his eyes fall on.

teach.h: PUT YE ON THE LORD JESUS CHRIST.
teach.b: Romans thirteen, in the King James Bible: "not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying. But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He says he didn't want or need to read further.
It was as if a light of peace flooded his heart, and the dark of doubt ran away. Alypius reads the next line, about welcoming the one who is weak in faith, and takes it for himself.

The two go straight inside to tell Monica, who, he says, leapt for joy. Years later, Augustine opened his Confessions with a line spoken to God: you made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.
That garden was where his restlessness met its rest.
One caution some Christian teachers add: this isn't a recipe for opening the Bible like a fortune cookie.
Augustine's moment came after years of searching, reading, arguing and being prayed for.

how: Augustine's conversion is remembered by Christians across the churches, and his line about the restless heart is often quoted. Some Christians read a short passage of scripture each day, and let one verse speak to them as he did.

games.q: you're Augustine, weeping under a fig tree. a child's voice next door keeps chanting, take up and read. what do you do?
o: ignore it. it's just children playing.
go back to the book of Paul's letters and read the first thing you see.
go and ask the child what they mean.
games.why: he hurries back, opens Paul's letters, and reads Romans 13: put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ. he didn't need to read further.

practice: Open any book nearby at random, a Bible if you have one, a novel, a poetry book, a cookbook, and read one sentence slowly. Don't hunt for a better one. Read it again.
Ask what it might say to you today; if nothing, that's fine, you've still stopped. If you pray, you can ask God to speak through what you read.

wordCard.voice: Tolle lege. Latin for take up and read, the words a child's voice seemed to chant in a Milan garden.

orig.note: Latin: take up, read. The child's chant Augustine heard in the garden (Confessions 8.12).

carryVoice: Your line: our heart is restless. Tomorrow, a rich man's son who preached to birds. Day ninety-two, done.
